## Three decisions, three different questions

A 3D picture combines a representation of the observations, a distance rule,
and a fitted approximation. Separating these decisions prevents a visually
striking plot from becoming its own evidence.

Here we hold the observations fixed and compare **L1 normalization with
Euclidean distance**, **max normalization with Euclidean distance**, and
**max normalization with L-infinity distance**. We measure each fit against
its own original-space distances. We do not compare ecological validity.

The [linf corner-geometry article](https://pgajer.github.io/linf/articles/simplex-corner-geometry.html)
explains how normalization alone can separate directions away from a dominant
taxon. This companion asks how much of the chosen distance geometry survives
an additional reduction to three dimensions.

## What is fitted, and what counts as success?

We use two examples: 48 reproducible four-part synthetic compositions and a
seeded sample of 300 distinct compositions from the 2,000 observations in
`linf::valencia2k`. The latter is a stratified teaching subset of VALENCIA data,
not a population-prevalence sample. See the
[dataset guide](https://pgajer.github.io/linf/articles/example-datasets.html).
All 178 taxon columns are retained. One distinct composition is one fit row;
no participant weighting or clinical outcome enters the analysis.

For each example and target, we fit three dimensions using `metric.mds()`
with the **SGD backend**, inverse-squared target-distance weights, 300 full
pair passes, and seeds 11, 29 and 47. Each seed gives one random start.
The Zheng schedule uses `schedule.epsilon=0.01`; checkpoints occur every ten
passes. The lowest achieved objective among these three runs supplies the
illustration. All seed results are reported, including budget exhaustion;
none is called a certified optimum.

There are only `r format(choose(nrow(z$P),2),big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE)` empirical pairs, so these examples use
full distance matrices and exact all-pairs evaluation. This is a teaching
choice, not a prescription for large datasets. See the
[sparse fitting guide](https://pgajer.github.io/grip/articles/sparse-metric-mds.html)
for larger collections.

The primary diagnostic is

\[
 E=100\sqrt{\frac{1}{|\mathcal P|}
       \sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal P}\left(\frac{d_{ij}-\delta_{ij}}{\delta_{ij}}\right)^2},
 \qquad d_{ij}=\|y_i-y_j\|_2.
\]

Here $\delta_{ij}>0$ is the selected target distance, $y_i$ is a fitted 3D
coordinate, and $\mathcal P$ contains all unordered pairs of distinct fit rows.
Zero means exact reproduction; 10% means an RMS relative error of 0.10,
**not** that every distance is accurate to 10%. No additional scale is fitted
when calculating this diagnostic. The solver's returned coordinates already
include its documented objective-based scale adjustment.

There is no universal acceptable percentage. A successful evaluation computes
the stated quantity correctly, reveals where errors occur, and exposes seed
sensitivity. A lower value for one target family does not show that its
normalization or metric is scientifically better than another.

## Construct the targets explicitly

For nonnegative rows with positive total, let $p=x/\sum_jx_j$ and
$q=x/\max_jx_j$. The targets are respectively
$\|p_i-p_j\|_2$, $\|q_i-q_j\|_2$, and
$\|q_i-q_j\|_\infty=\max_k|q_{ik}-q_{jk}|$.
Max normalization and L-infinity distance are separate operations.

```{r target-recipe, eval=FALSE}
P <- X / rowSums(X)
Q <- X / apply(X, 1, max)
D1 <- as.matrix(dist(P))
D2 <- as.matrix(dist(Q))
D3 <- as.matrix(dist(Q, method = 'maximum'))
fit <- metric.mds(distance.matrix=D3, dim=3, backend='sgd',
  pair.weights='inverse_squared', init='random', n.init=1,
  max.iter=300, seed=11,
  sgd.control=list(scheduler='zheng',schedule.epsilon=.01,checkpoint.every=10))
```

`distance.matrix` uses these values directly: no neighbor graph or shortest
paths replace them. Remove duplicate normalized rows before using
inverse-squared weights, and retain the mapping back to original observations.
Near-zero positive targets are retained, not floored; they can make relative
error demanding. In this empirical subset, the smallest positive target in
each family is:

```{r target-minima}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Method=names(targets),Minimum=vapply(targets,
  function(D) min(D[lower.tri(D)]),numeric(1))),digits=6,row.names=FALSE)
```

## A small example with a known reference

Four-part L1 compositions lie in a three-dimensional affine hyperplane, so
their Euclidean distances admit an exact 3D representation. We can construct
one directly using an orthonormal basis, independent of MDS. Max-normalized
points can span several faces in four dimensions, and L-infinity targets
need not be Euclidean even before reducing dimension.

```{r exact-toy}
H<-qr.Q(qr(cbind(rep(1,4),diag(4)[,1:3]))) [,-1,drop=FALSE]
exact<-z$toy%*%H
exact.error<-study_score(exact,toy.targets[[1]])[1]
stopifnot(exact.error<1e-10)
knitr::kable(toy$scores[,1:6],digits=3,row.names=FALSE,
  col.names=c("Method","Seed","RMS (%)","Short (%)","Long (%)","Median absolute (%)"))
```

The independently constructed exact L1 representation has RMS relative error
below $10^{-10}$ percent. Any larger error in the fitted L1 rows above is
optimization error under this budget. For the other targets, an observed
residual can combine dimensional incompatibility and optimization error; these
runs do not separate the two or establish the best achievable stress.

## Results on the bundled microbiome example

```{r all-seeds}
knitr::kable(real$scores[,1:6],digits=2,row.names=FALSE,
  col.names=c("Method","Seed","RMS (%)","Short (%)","Long (%)","Median absolute (%)"))
```

The best observed RMS errors are **`r paste(round(vapply(names(targets),function(m) min(real$scores$RMS_percent[real$scores$Method==m]),numeric(1)),2),collapse="%, ")`%**,
in the method order shown above. These are achieved errors for different target
families, not a ranking of biological usefulness. All 18 runs (both examples)
ended at the iteration limit. Values printed as zero are rounded, not a claim
of exact numerical equality.

The columns for shortest and longest distances use each target's own bottom
and top distance deciles, including boundary ties. Their membership can differ
between target families. Every fit is checked against every pair; this measures
training-distance fidelity, not generalization to unseen samples.

```{r seed-variation, fig.cap="Each point is one recorded seed. Lower is better only relative to the target family on the same axis; differences between methods also reflect different distance geometries."}
op<-par(mar=c(8,4,1,1))
plot(NA,xlim=c(.6,3.4),ylim=range(c(0,real$scores$RMS_percent)),xaxt='n',
     xlab='',ylab='RMS relative error (%)')
axis(1,1:3,names(targets),las=2)
for(i in 1:3) points(rep(i,3)+c(-.08,0,.08),real$scores$RMS_percent[real$scores$Method==names(targets)[i]],
  pch=16,col=c('#0072B2','#D55E00','#009E73')[i])
par(op)
```

## Where are distances distorted?

The following plots use the best of the three recorded starts for each
method. Every empirical pair is shown. The diagonal is exact preservation;
vertical spread indicates errors hidden by a single RMS number.

```{r distance-plots, fig.height=3.5, fig.cap="Target distance versus fitted Euclidean distance in 3D, in each target's own units. Axes within each panel have the same range."}
op<-par(mfrow=c(1,3),mar=c(4,4,3,1))
for(m in names(targets)) {
  t<-as.numeric(as.dist(targets[[m]])); d<-as.numeric(dist(real$best[[m]]$coords))
  lim<-range(c(0,t,d))
  plot(t,d,pch=16,cex=.2,col=adjustcolor('#0072B2',alpha.f=.12),
       xlim=lim,ylim=lim,asp=1,main=m,xlab='Target distance',ylab='3D distance')
  abline(0,1,col='#D55E00',lwd=2)
}
par(op)
```

## Explore the three fitted views

Drag to rotate and scroll to zoom. All views use the same observations, colors,
sphere radius, camera and coordinate limits. We remove translation and align
orientations to the first fit using an orthogonal transformation; **we do not
rescale the drawings**. Alignment preserves all fitted pair distances and
cannot remove deformation. Axes are arbitrary embedding coordinates.
Different overall sizes may reflect different target-distance units.

```{r make-widgets, include=FALSE}
widgets<-study_widgets(lapply(real$best,`[[`,'coords'),z$groups,
  paste(names(targets),'— best of three recorded full SGD fits'))
```

### L1 normalization, Euclidean distance

```{r view-l1, echo=FALSE}
widgets[[1]]
```

### Max normalization, Euclidean distance

```{r view-max-euclidean, echo=FALSE}
widgets[[2]]
```

### Max normalization, L-infinity distance

```{r view-max-linf, echo=FALSE}
widgets[[3]]
```

A visible arm or gap is a feature to investigate in the original data and
selected targets. It is not, by itself, evidence of a community boundary.
Colors describe the original dominant taxon; changing normalization or fitting
does not reassign these labels.

## Reproduce and interpret the comparison

This is a website article for the development version of grip with direct
`distance.matrix` support. It requires linf's bundled data and ivue/rgl for
interactive figures. The source-visible `embedding-study.R` beside this
article contains data selection, scoring, fitting, and alignment functions.
From a source checkout, run `make embedding-fidelity-vignette`.
The on-demand renderer records source fingerprints, session information,
selected rows and every fit's settings; cached fits are keyed by inputs,
solver settings and implementation fingerprints. It does not publish the site.

The article reports the specified 300-pass experiment without extending runs
until a preferred picture appears. More starts or longer schedules would be
new experiments. The examples do not determine an optimal normalization,
certify convergence, or provide participant-level uncertainty estimates.
